title: Backtracking
summary: Build candidates choice by choice; undo when a partial path fails.

parts.rule: Backtracking constructs an answer one decision at a time. After each choice, recurse into the next decision slot. When a partial path cannot succeed, undo that choice and try the sibling option. Prune as soon as a constraint is broken so doomed subtrees are never explored. The call stack (or an explicit path array) is the record of choices in flight.
parts.why: Permutation, combination, and board-constraint problems explode if you build every candidate and filter afterward. Backtracking is disciplined search with undo. Typical bugs: forgetting to revert shared state, pruning only at the leaves, and using backtracking where overlapping subproblems want dynamic programming instead.
parts.example: Permutations of [1, 2, 3]. Begin with path []. Take 1 → [1]; take 2 → [1,2]; take 3 → [1,2,3] and record; pop 3; pop 2; take 3 → [1,3]; take 2 → [1,3,2] and record; unwind to []. Continue with 2 as the first element until all six orders are stored. A used-set blocks picking the same index twice. For subset sums aiming at 5 from [1, 2, 3], branch on include versus skip; cut a branch when the running sum exceeds 5. Path [2,3] hits the target and is recorded; path [1,2,3] dies mid-way once the sum passes five. For a 2x2 letter grid searching for word "ab", try each start cell, walk to unused neighbors matching the next letter, and mark cells visited then unmark on return so sibling paths can reuse them.
parts.use: Use backtracking for permutations, combinations, queens-style boards, grid word search, and small constraint problems with strong pruning. Use it when you must list feasible solutions, not only compute an optimal numeric cost. Prefer it when n is tiny and the constraint check is cheap.
parts.refuse: Do not backtrack on large n without pruning — the tree is exponential. Do not choose it when a greedy proof or a DP recurrence already solves the optimization. Do not mutate a shared buffer without undoing before the next sibling. Do not enumerate all permutations when only a count is required and a closed formula exists.

body:
Rule. Backtracking constructs an answer one decision at a time. After each choice, recurse into the next decision slot. When a partial path cannot succeed, undo that choice and try the sibling option. Prune as soon as a constraint is broken so doomed subtrees are never explored. The call stack (or an explicit path array) is the record of choices in flight.

Why it matters. Permutation, combination, and board-constraint problems explode if you build every candidate and filter afterward. Backtracking is disciplined search with undo. Typical bugs: forgetting to revert shared state, pruning only at the leaves, and using backtracking where overlapping subproblems want dynamic programming instead.

Worked example. Permutations of [1, 2, 3]. Begin with path []. Take 1 → [1]; take 2 → [1,2]; take 3 → [1,2,3] and record; pop 3; pop 2; take 3 → [1,3]; take 2 → [1,3,2] and record; unwind to []. Continue with 2 as the first element until all six orders are stored. A used-set blocks picking the same index twice. For subset sums aiming at 5 from [1, 2, 3], branch on include versus skip; cut a branch when the running sum exceeds 5. Path [2,3] hits the target and is recorded; path [1,2,3] dies mid-way once the sum passes five. For a 2x2 letter grid searching for word "ab", try each start cell, walk to unused neighbors matching the next letter, and mark cells visited then unmark on return so sibling paths can reuse them.

[[diagram:tree-choices]]

When to use. Use backtracking for permutations, combinations, queens-style boards, grid word search, and small constraint problems with strong pruning. Use it when you must list feasible solutions, not only compute an optimal numeric cost. Prefer it when n is tiny and the constraint check is cheap.

When to refuse. Do not backtrack on large n without pruning — the tree is exponential. Do not choose it when a greedy proof or a DP recurrence already solves the optimization. Do not mutate a shared buffer without undoing before the next sibling. Do not enumerate all permutations when only a count is required and a closed formula exists.
